questions.question: Explain Down's process for the extraction of sodium.
questions.solution:
**Down's process:** Electrolysis of molten NaCl (with CaCl₂ added to lower melting point from 801°C to ~600°C).

- Anode (graphite): 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂↑ + 2e⁻
- Cathode (iron): Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na↓
- Na metal collects under a steel bell
- CaCl₂ addition lowers melting point and increases conductivity
questions.knowledgeNote: Sodium cannot be extracted from aqueous solution because Na⁺ is harder to reduce than H₂O.
questions.answer: **Downs process — electrolysis of molten NaCl.** **Why not aqueous brine:** water is reduced at the cathode before Na⁺, so metallic sodium requires the *dry molten* salt; **why the mixture:** pure NaCl melts at 801 °C (wasteful and corrosive), so it is mixed with **CaCl₂ (and NaF)** which lowers the melting point to ~600 °C and improves conductivity. **The cell:** a steel tank lined with refractory brick; a **graphite anode** in the centre releases **Cl₂** (collected in an inverted funnel/hood); a **ring-shaped steel cathode** surrounds it, around which molten **sodium** collects (density lower than the melt) and rises up a pipe into a collector. A **steel-gauze diaphragm** between the electrodes keeps the Na from the Cl₂ (they would recombine — and Na + Cl₂ is violent). **Reactions:** cathode: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na (molten metal); anode: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻; overall: 2NaCl --electrolysis--> 2Na + Cl₂. The CaCl₂ is not reduced (Ca²⁺ needs a higher potential than Na⁺ at these conditions). Calcium contamination of the sodium is controlled by keeping the temperature just above Na's melting point, where Ca's solubility in Na is low. **Deep point:** the process is three engineering answers to one chemistry — lower the melting point, separate the products, and let density do the collection.

questions.question: Compare the extraction of sodium by the Downs cell with the extraction of magnesium by the electrolysis of fused magnesium chloride. Give the electrode reactions and state the physical state of each metal obtained.
questions.solution:
**Downs cell — sodium (NaCl melted with CaCl₂ at about 850 °C).**

Sodium is more reactive than magnesium, so its chloride must be reduced by electrolysis, not by carbon.

Cathode: $\text{Na}^+ + e^- \rightarrow \text{Na}$. The working temperature of 850 °C is above the m.p. of sodium ($97.8$ °C), so **liquid sodium** floats up and is tapped through a separate pipe, away from the chlorine.

Anode: $2\text{Cl}^- \rightarrow \text{Cl}_2 + 2e^-$. Chlorine gas rises and escapes; the iron diaphragm prevents it from mixing with the sodium.

$$2\text{NaCl(l)} \rightarrow 2\text{Na(l)} + \text{Cl}_2(g)$$

**Electrolysis of fused MgCl₂ (about 750 °C).**

Cathode: $\text{Mg}^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{Mg}$. Magnesium melts at $650$ °C but the bath is kept hotter, so **solid magnesium** is deposited and scraped off, protecting it from further oxidation.

Anode: $2\text{Cl}^- \rightarrow \text{Cl}_2 + 2e^-$.

$$\text{MgCl}_2(l) \rightarrow \text{Mg(s)} + \text{Cl}_2(g)$$

**Contrast.** Both need electrolysis of a fused (anhydrous) halide and both yield chlorine at the anode, but sodium is obtained as a liquid (higher operating temperature) whereas magnesium is obtained as a solid (lower operating temperature).
questions.knowledgeNote: Both metals are extracted by electrolysis of fused chlorides; sodium comes off liquid, magnesium as a solid.
questions.answer: **Downs cell (sodium):** electrolyte **molten NaCl + CaCl₂** (m.p. lowered to ~600 °C); graphite anode: **2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻**; steel cathode: **Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na (liquid metal)**, collected by floating; steel-gauze diaphragm separates the products; metal obtained **molten (liquid)**. **Fused MgCl₂ cell (magnesium):** electrolyte **molten (fused) MgCl₂** (often with NaCl/KCl to lower the melting point); graphite anode: **2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻**; steel cathode: **Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mg (molten metal)**, which floats on the denser electrolyte and is skimmed; chlorine is a by-product at both cells. **Comparison:** the chemistry is identical (cation reduced, chloride oxidised — both metals come out **molten** because the electrolyte must be fused); the differences are operational — Downs uses a mixed electrolyte purely to lower the melting point and a diaphragm to stop Na + Cl₂ recombination, while the Mg cell's melt runs hotter (~700 °C) and skims its metal off the surface. **Deep point:** both cells are the same electrochemistry in different vessels — the syllabus point is that reactive metals (Na, Mg, Al) are won from their **molten** compounds, never from solution.
